title: Most Black Friday Deals Aren't Deals
summary: In 2012, J.C. Penney stopped its endless sales and lost $985 million. Here's why stores keep crossed-out prices, what US and Canadian rules say, and how to check a Black Friday deal.

hooks.hook: In 2012, the man who built the Apple Stores took over J.C. Penney and promised no more endless sales.
At 21 of 25 big US chains, the 'sale' price is just the price.
The crossed-out price isn't the price. It's the bait.

sources: J.C. Penney's new pricing (Jan 2012): "We had 590 unique promotions [online and in stores] last year in 365 days"; "less than 1 percent" of sales at full price; towels "$10 but always discounted to $4 will be priced at $4": https://www.dallasnews.com/business/retail/2012/01/25/j-c-penneys-new-pricing-explained

J.C. Penney fiscal 2012: "lost $985 million"; "Total sales decreased 24.8 percent"; Ron Johnson: our customer "loves a sale, at times she loves a coupon, and she always wants a reference price" (JCK, Feb 28, 2013): https://www.jckonline.com/editorial-article/jc-penney-lost-nearly-1-billion-in-2012/
After Johnson left (April 2013): "Overnight, the list prices for some items rose 60% or more" (TIME): https://business.time.com/?p=98656
Johnson ran Apple's retail stores before J.C. Penney; ousted April 2013 (Fortune, Mar 20, 2014): https://fortune.com/2014/03/20/how-to-fail-in-business-while-really-really-trying/

Consumers' Checkbook, Sale Fail 2025 (Nov 13, 2025): 25 national chains, weekly for 24 weeks; "21 out of 25" showed the same sale prices more than half the time; JCPenney among stores where "most of the items tracked ... were always or almost always on sale"; only Apple, Costco and Dell "consistently conducted legitimate discounts"; Kevin Brasler quote: https://www.checkbook.org/pdfDocs/doc/Sale_Fail_2025_press_release.pdf

Which? (UK), Nov 25, 2025: 175 products at eight retailers tracked six months before and after Black Friday 2024; 83% cheaper or the same price at least once outside the sales period; no deal was at its cheapest of the year on Black Friday itself; toothbrush "RRP £50" applied on only 13 days in the prior six months: https://www.which.co.uk/policy-and-insight/article/dont-believe-the-hype-most-black-friday-deals-the-same-price-or-cheaper-at-other-times-of-the-year-which-finds-a3TbD5x5KADs

US FTC Guides Against Deceptive Pricing, 16 CFR 233.1 (1967): a former price should be one at which "the product was openly and actively offered for sale, for a reasonably substantial period of time": https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-233

Competition Bureau Canada, ordinary selling price (volume and time tests): https://competition-bureau.canada.ca/deceptive-marketing-practices/types-deceptive-marketing-practices/ordinary-selling-price

Amazon agreed to pay a $1,000,000 penalty in Canada (Jan 2017) after the Bureau found its list prices "were not substantiated": https://www.legal500.com/intelligence/canada/antitrust-competition-law/amazon-to-pay-$1000000-to-competition-bureau-for-unsubstantiated-sales-prices-global-advertising-lawyers-alliance-gala

scenes.narration: In {2012,|twenty twelve,} the man who built the Apple Stores took over J.C. Penney, and made a promise. No more endless sales. Just fair prices, every day.
That year, sales fell by about a quarter, and the company lost {$985 million.|nine hundred eighty-five million dollars.} By April {2013,|twenty thirteen,} he was out.
Shoppers didn't want fair prices. They wanted to feel like they were winning. And every Black Friday, stores sell them that feeling.
Part one. The price nobody paid.
Before the change, J.C. Penney ran {590|five hundred ninety} different promotions in a single year.

data.label: promotions in one year (2011)
data.source: J.C. Penney, via Dallas Morning News, Jan 2012

scenes.narration: And less than one percent of its sales happened at full price.
One towel was listed at {$10,|ten dollars,} but it almost always sold for {$4.|four dollars.} So the new boss simply priced it at {$4.|four dollars.}
Same towel. Same four dollars. But now there was no ten-dollar price to beat, and the shoppers stayed away.
A year later, he admitted it. Their customer loves a sale, at times she loves a coupon, and she always wants a reference price.

data.quote: ...loves a sale, at times she loves a coupon, and she always wants a *reference price*.

scenes.narration: A reference price is the crossed-out number on the tag. It isn't there to tell you what the thing costs. It's there to make the real price feel like a win.
If you like seeing the receipts behind everyday prices, subscribe. New ones every Tuesday and Friday.
Part two. Always on sale.
So how common is this today? A US consumer group, Consumers' Checkbook, checked prices at {25|twenty-five} national chains, once a week, for {24 weeks.|twenty-four weeks.}
At {21|twenty-one} of the {25,|twenty-five,} the same sale prices were up more than half the time.
Only three ran real discounts consistently. Apple, Costco and Dell.
Its editor put it bluntly. Seeing fifty or sixty percent off a regular price doesn't mean anything.

data.quote: Seeing 50 percent or 60 percent off a regular price *doesn't mean anything*.

scenes.narration: Part three. The Black Friday test.
And on Black Friday itself? A British consumer group tracked {175|one hundred seventy-five} products for a full year around the sales. Not one was at its lowest price of the year on Black Friday.
In fact, {83 percent|eighty-three percent} were the same price or cheaper at some other time.

data.label: same price or cheaper at other times

scenes.narration: In the US, the rule is from {1967,|nineteen sixty-seven,} and it's vague. A crossed-out price should be one the product was openly and actively offered at, for a reasonably substantial period of time. It never says how many days.

data.quote: ...openly and actively offered for sale, for a *reasonably substantial* period of time
data.who: US FTC, Guides Against Deceptive Pricing

scenes.narration: Canada has an actual test. In {2017,|twenty seventeen,} Amazon paid a {$1 million|one million dollar} penalty there, because it couldn't back up the list prices it compared against.
And J.C. Penney? After he left, the sales came back. Some list prices jumped {60 percent|sixty percent} or more, overnight.
In {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} that same consumer group listed J.C. Penney among the stores where most items were always, or almost always, on sale.
So this Black Friday, ignore the crossed-out number. Look up what the thing cost last month. If it's the same, it isn't a deal. Trust me. I'm a price tag.
The crossed-out number isn't the price. It's the bait. Next time: why Starbucks wants your money before you order.
